records.title: The Visitation (with predella scenes)
records.summary: Two women embrace under a grand stone arch; a predella below connects the Annunciation, Nativity, and Presentation in the Temple.
records.context: The central Visitation is simple and clear. The smaller painted scenes along its bottom trace other moments in Jesus' early life. Mary is the younger visitor, Elizabeth the older pregnant relative.
history_paragraphs: Albertinelli painted the Visitation in 1503, arranging the meeting beneath a carefully measured Renaissance arch. The two women fill the central space, making their embrace the focal point.

The Uffizi describes a predella beneath the main scene with the Annunciation, Nativity, and Presentation of Jesus. These are separate events in the Gospel story and should not be mistaken for different stages of the Visitation.

Mary and Elizabeth are not recognized by fixed robe colors. The meeting, their relative ages, and the context in Luke help identify them. The painting was commissioned for an oratory connected with devotion to the Visitation.
learning_points: the relationship of Mary and Elizabeth

records.title: The Meeting of Mary and Elizabeth
records.museum: Frederiksborg Castle Museum of National History, Denmark (verify exact object)
records.summary: Elizabeth appears at the doorway above steps with arms opened wide; Mary is the younger figure coming to visit.
records.context: A powerful example where Mary and Elizabeth are not yet embracing. Identify the older expectant hostess and the younger arriving visitor through the unfolding action.
history_paragraphs: The Danish painter Carl Bloch presents the Visitation in a vertical composition, emphasizing the distance across the steps rather than depicting the embrace at its climax.
The raised arms of the older woman express welcome; the younger visitor comes from below. This is the same event that other artists depict with two figures already embracing.
The painting is a valuable test of transferring recognition. If children only memorize that the older figure is on the right or that the women embrace, this composition challenges those shortcuts.

records.title: The Visitation with Mary Jacobi and Mary Salome
records.summary: Mary bends toward a kneeling Elizabeth. Two additional named holy women stand at the outer edges, identified in the Louvre catalogue as Mary Jacobi (left) and Mary Salome (right).
records.context: The Louvre records inscriptions on the arch naming the two side saints. Their names come from written evidence and the artwork's history, not uniquely identifiable dress or poses.
history_paragraphs: Domenico Ghirlandaio painted this altarpiece in 1491 for Lorenzo Tornabuoni's chapel in Florence. The scene is framed by a monumental classical arch.

The central pair is Mary, who bends to greet her older relative Elizabeth. Two further female saints flank them. The Louvre identifies the left saint as Mary Jacobi and the right as Mary Salome; the upper inscriptions are especially useful evidence for these identifications.

This painting teaches a historical skill: some figures cannot reliably be named from clothing alone. An inscription or documented dedication can identify someone more securely than a guessed attribute.

records.title: The Visitation (Scrovegni Chapel)
records.summary: Mary and Elizabeth embrace at the entrance to a building with other women nearby, showing the emotional encounter in a simple narrative style.
records.context: The women may be accompanied by attendants; those women should not automatically be given names as saints.
history_paragraphs: Giotto painted the Visitation among scenes from Mary's life in the Scrovegni Chapel in Padua. The whole chapel organizes biblical stories into a larger sequence.
The women exchange an intimate greeting in front of a portico. The quiet gestures make their relationship more important than the surrounding architecture.
Other women in the scene are usually described as attendants. Their presence contributes to the story but is not proof that they are additional named saints.

records.title: The Visitation (Carmignano)
records.museum: Church of San Michele e Francesco, Carmignano
records.summary: Mary and Elizabeth embrace in the foreground. Two women stand facing the viewer; their specific identities are not securely established.
records.context: The background figures have sometimes been interpreted as doubled images of the main women or attendants. We should not test them as named saints.
history_paragraphs: Pontormo's unusual arrangement places four monumental women against a narrow street. The two in profile embrace, while the figures behind them look directly toward us.
The bright and unexpected colors, elongated shapes and tightly interwoven arms distinguish this work from the balanced Renaissance scenes of Albertinelli and Ghirlandaio.

The two rear figures have been interpreted as attendants or symbolic doubles of Mary and Elizabeth. Their names are not securely established, making this painting ideal for learning to distinguish evidence from speculation.

records.title: The Visitation
records.summary: Light falls on the greeting between Mary and Elizabeth. Zechariah approaches with help at the left; other attendants and animals animate the scene.
records.context: The older man is identified as Zechariah through the Visitation setting and museum descriptions. Age or a beard alone is not enough to identify him.
history_paragraphs: Rembrandt painted the Visitation in 1640, placing the action within a shaded courtyard. Unlike the bright Italian examples, most of the picture remains dark.
Light falls on the women, suggesting the importance of their meeting. Zechariah, Elizabeth's husband and father of John the Baptist, appears at the left, helped down steps by a younger figure.

The painting contains additional people and animals, including a peacock. In Christian art peacocks have sometimes been used to suggest immortality. They belong to the artist's symbolism, not a detail described by Luke.

records.title: The Visitation
records.summary: Mary and Elizabeth stand together in a landscape; the future Baptism of Christ appears in the distant background.
records.context: John the Baptist is present in the background depiction as an adult, not physically beside the two pregnant women at their greeting.
history_paragraphs: Raphael designed this Visitation for a chapel in L'Aquila, with workshop participation often acknowledged in accounts of its execution.
The two women occupy the foreground and share a tender greeting. The landscape behind them contains a second biblical episode: the future Baptism of Jesus by John the Baptist.

The artist thus shows events separated by decades in one composition. That artistic choice connects Elizabeth's unborn son with the work he will later perform, but it is not a single moment recorded by Luke.

records.title: The Visitation
records.summary: Mary approaches Elizabeth outside her house after a journey through the hills; a small Zechariah can be seen in the background.
records.context: Their gestures to each other's bodies emphasize the pregnancies. Zechariah is small and only identifiable using the setting and source record.
history_paragraphs: Rogier van der Weyden places the Visitation outside a house in an open landscape, showing the road by which Mary may have traveled.
Mary and Elizabeth touch each other as they greet. A path winds through the hills and leads our eyes back toward the building, reinforcing Luke's account of Mary's journey.
The small figure of Zechariah appears outside Elizabeth's house in the background. Here his identification depends on the house and story context, not on a unique object.

records.title: The Visitation (wing of The Descent from the Cross)
records.summary: A narrow panel in Rubens's Descent from the Cross triptych shows Mary bearing the unborn Jesus when she visits Elizabeth.
records.context: Interesting theological comparison: the altarpiece's wider theme is bearing Christ. Reproduction is too narrow/low-resolution for new first-pass quiz images.
history_paragraphs: Rubens painted this Visitation as a wing of a large triptych for Antwerp Cathedral. The central subject of the altarpiece is the Descent from the Cross.
In the side wing Mary carries Jesus within her body during the Visitation; in the other wing Simeon holds the infant at the Presentation. The altarpiece connects several meanings of carrying Christ.
The local reproduction is relatively small and narrow. Preserve it for optional art history and comparison rather than asking children to identify tiny details in it.
